claims.text: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC solid solution.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has limited room-temperature compressive plasticity.
The high Mo content of equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is responsible for its reduced plasticity.
Reducing the Mo content will lower the overall electronegativity difference in NbZrTiHfMo.
Ta is less electronegative than Mo and can serve as a partial substitute for Mo.
Partial substitution of Mo with a less electronegative element will reduce the alloy's electronegativity contrast.
Lower electronegativity difference reduces localized bond rigidity.
Reducing Mo or substituting it with a less electronegative element decreases bonding heterogeneity.
Reduced bond rigidity and bonding heterogeneity facilitate dislocation motion.
Increased dislocation mobility improves room-temperature compressive plasticity.
After moderate Mo reduction or substitution, sufficient lattice distortion will remain to sustain high yield strength.
The modified alloy will exhibit increased compressive strain to failure relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo.
The modified alloy will retain a compressive yield strength within approximately 10–15% of 1719 MPa.
Moderate Mo reduction or substitution can improve plasticity without disrupting the BCC phase.
Excessive Mo reduction or substitution may destabilize the BCC phase.
Excessive Mo reduction or substitution may cause a significant loss of yield strength.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that excessive modification may predictably cause phase instability and lies outside the claimed beneficial regime, whereas the falsification rule treats loss of the BCC phase in the modified alloys as an unconditional falsifier. A phase loss at an excessive modification level would therefore both conform to the stated boundary and purportedly falsify the hypothesis.
